newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian children at risk from low vaccine rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian children at risk from low vaccine rates.

text.p: Australian health officials have warned Australian children's lives are at risk from epidemics of whooping cough and measles because of immunisation rates which are among the worst in the world.
Officials say four children have died from whooping cough in the past three months, a significant rise on official expectations of only one death every two years.

Public health doctor Gavin Frost said on Wednesday notified cases of whooping cough had risen in South Australia to 186 in November 1996 from 41 in August 1996, in New South Wales to 154 from 62 and in Victoria to 315 from 93.
"That's the definition of an epidemic", he told Reuters.
Official figures also show 42 deaths due to measles or complications have been reported in the past two years, which Frost said was way above rates in comparable Western nations.
"Deaths from measles should no longer occur," he said.

Health Minister Michael Wooldrige said this week only 53 percent of Australian children were fully vaccinated against infectious diseases, one of the world's lowest rates, compared to 100 percent in Indonesia and 90 percent in China and Vietnam.
Wooldridge said one in every 4,000 children not immunised against whooping cough was likely to die.
"Now that is a pretty frightening figure when you have got so many kids unimmunised," he said.

The Australian Medical Association (AMA) said complacency was the main cause of such a low rate of immunisation, with research showing only two percent of parents refusing on religious or medical grounds.
Australian children are offered free immunisation against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, haemophilus influenza type B, measles, mumps and rubella.
Wooldridge next month launchs a national strategy to boost immunisation rates.
